---
title: "PlasticIceSheet.jl"
subtitle: "Fast, AD-friendly perfectly-plastic ice-sheet reconstruction"
---

`PlasticIceSheet.jl` reconstructs a perfectly plastic, steady-state ice sheet from three
inputs: a grounded-ice **mask**, a **bed elevation** $z_b$ and a **basal shear stress**
$\tau_b$. It returns the ice **surface** $z_s$ and **thickness** $H$, with no time stepping,
no climate and no ice dynamics.

It is a simplification and modernization of ICESHEET 2.0 by Evan Gowan and colleagues
([source code](https://github.com/evangowan/icesheet);
[Gowan et al., 2016, *Geosci. Model Dev.*](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1673-2016);
[Gowan et al., 2021, *Nat. Commun.*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-21469-w)). The core
physics, one published equation, is retained. The recursive flowline, crossover and saddle
machinery of ICESHEET (about 2,600 lines) is replaced by a grid solver of a few hundred lines
([Algorithms §10](algorithms.qmd#sec-dropped)).

The package is meant as a first-guess tool next to a dynamic ice-sheet model (e.g.,
[Yelmo](https://github.com/palma-ice/yelmo)) and an independent GIA and sea-level solver.
Typical uses are to initialize a spin-up, to provide a surface for an SMB model, or to serve as
a relaxation target.

## The idea

Under the perfectly plastic, steady-state assumption the basal shear stress balances the
gravitational driving stress, which is set by the geometry:

$$
\tau_b = \tau_d = \rho_i\, g\, H\, |\nabla z_s| .
$$

Rearranging for the surface slope gives the equation we solve,

$$
|\nabla z_s| = \frac{\tau_b}{\rho_i\, g\, (z_s - z_b)} ,
$$

a static Hamilton–Jacobi equation. It is discretized with a monotone upwind scheme and
solved by fast sweeping in one pass over the grid, bed relief included. Saddles, domes and
coalescing ice caps follow from the upwind (viscosity) solution without flowline tracing or
saddle detection ([Algorithms §1–6](algorithms.qmd)).

Two extensions build on the fixed geometry. A DIVA closure recovers what perfect plasticity
discards, a depth-averaged velocity and a first-order surface mass balance
([§8](algorithms.qmd#sec-closures)). The same flux law then drives the geometry *from* an
SMB instead of a yield stress, by solving steady mass conservation on the prescribed margin
([§9](algorithms.qmd#sec-reconstruct)).

## Quick start

```julia
using PlasticIceSheet

nx, ny = 100, 100
dx = dy = 2000.0                                       # grid spacing (m)
z_b  = zeros(nx, ny)                                   # bed elevation (m)
mask = [hypot(i - 50.5, j - 50.5) <= 40 for i in 1:nx, j in 1:ny]
τ_b  = 1.0e5                                           # basal shear stress (Pa)

z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)                 # mode = :surface (default)
```

A solve on a 300 × 300 grid takes a few milliseconds. The result is differentiable with
respect to $\tau_b$, which enables gradient-based [inversion](inversion.qmd). See
[Usage](usage.qmd) for the options, the closures and the examples.

`PlasticIceSheet.jl` is MIT-licensed. A dependency-free Fortran port for coupling into
Fortran models is available as [PlasticIceSheet](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet).
